sections.text: This is what our Monday produces. Twenty-three of these in three weeks. Not one of them was ever made.
Five steps. Collect, score, shortlist, strike out, hand over. Four of them run without anyone touching anything.

The process is not broken where the money went. It is broken at the step where a plan is supposed to become somebody's job, and that step has no name and no owner.

strategy.audience: Non-technical small-business leader, AI level 0-6 of 10 (POSITIONING.md §4): an owner, operations lead or team lead in a 5-50 person company responsible for one repeated process. Specifically whoever runs the weekly planning ritual.
strategy.concept: We take our own weekly planning ritual apart step by step on screen, with the artefact each step produces and the real count beside it, and show that the leak is not in any of the four automated steps but in the fifth - the handover, which has no name, no owner and, in three weeks, nothing recorded against it at all.

filter.ai_boundary: The machine can collect, score, shortlist and draft. Deciding which items are real and who owns each one stays with a person - in our week that is one of us on Monday - and no step downstream may begin without that name attached.
filter.friction: All the effort goes into producing the list, and the list is not where the process fails. It fails at the handover, where no name is attached, so nothing downstream can start and nobody notices that nothing did.
filter.next_action: Take last week's list, write the owner's name next to every item, and count how many are blank.
filter.process: The recurring weekly planning meeting or run that produces a list of things to do - the Monday list, the sprint board, the shortlist of jobs for the week - in any business where the same ritual repeats and produces the same kind of list.

strategy.objective: Get one viewer to take last week's list, write an owner's name next to every line, and count how many lines come back blank.
strategy.promise: A five-step teardown of a weekly ritual, with the real counts, and the exact step where a plan stops being anybody's job.
strategy.rationale: The corpus states a problem in only 64 of 264 reels and never takes apart a process the author runs (I-17). RULES.md §2 names our own processes as the only Teardown source available from day one, and the format's second pass criterion - a reason to forward - is carried by the count itself: twenty-three plans, nothing produced. The reel opens on the artefact rather than on a face, because openings spent on the audience carry median robust_z 0.67 against 1.36 (I-06).

traceability.evidence_summary: Every number is our own and reproducible from data/radar.db: 23 planning cards across three weeks (5 / 9 / 9 on 3, 7 and 10 September 2026), a person struck out 9 of them, three source reels came back a second time in a later week, the whole machine run took 65 minutes, and the table that would record a produced reel has zero rows. That last figure is the reason to forward it, which is the Teardown format's second pass criterion. The corpus states a problem in only 64 of 264 reels and never takes apart a process the author runs (I-17), so a step-by-step of the author's own week with the failure point named is unrepresented. The references contribute shape only: DYuivWzSj5k (50.8 shares/1k, fourth in the 40-reel pool) the recognisable-weekday entry and the node-with-a-counter treatment, DZLDk9ySi-7 (41.9 shares, 45.4 saves/1k) the pain-as-acts list and the stacked-step layout, Db9MT-axxcO (47.9 shares and 68.9 saves per 1 000, third-best combined pair in the analysis-ready corpus, on a lift of only 1.62x) the beat clock and the artefact-in-hand framing, DbbA7wwTIZ8 the tightly bounded next action.
traceability.original_synthesis: The process is ours, we may show it without anyone's permission - which RULES.md §2 names as the only Teardown source available from day one - and the finding is unflattering: the four steps we automated all work, and the one that does not is the step nobody built anything for. The five-step map with a real count against each step, ending on a count of zero, is ours and appears in no reference.
traceability.why_better_than_generic: A generic process teardown would find the leak in the manual step and sell automation for it. This one automates four steps successfully and still produces nothing, which locates the failure in the handover instead - the part no tool is being sold for. It also refuses the two numbers it does not have: how long the human step takes, and whether naming an owner fixes anything.
